title: Insulation Calculator: Batts and Blown-In by R-Value
description: Work out batts or bags of blown-in insulation by area and target R-value, with Energy Star targets and a worked attic example.
seoTitle: Insulation Calculator: Batts and Blown-In by R-Value

cover.alt: Blown-in insulation being sprayed between attic joists from a hose

keywords: how much insulation do I need
takeaways: Energy Star attic targets run from R-30 in Zone 1 to R-49 to R-60 in Zones 5 to 8 for an uninsulated attic.
Blown-in bags needed = attic area in sq ft x bags per 1,000 sq ft from the bag chart, divided by 1,000.
Existing insulation counts, so subtract its R-value from your target before you buy anything.
body:
For a 1,000 sq ft attic (93 sq m) taken to R-49, plan on about 27 bags of blown-in insulation, or about 10 bags of R-19 batts per layer. The exact count comes from your area, your target R-value, and the coverage on the bag. This guide shows the formula and how to check a quote.

## The formula for batts and blown-in

Start with the area. Measure length x width for each section and add the sections together. If the space is an odd shape, our [square footage calculator](/blog/square-footage-calculator/) handles L-shapes and triangles.

**For blown-in: bags = area in sq ft / 1,000 x bags per 1,000 sq ft at your target R-value.**

**For batts: bags = area in sq ft / sq ft covered per bag on the label.**

Use the chart on the exact product you will buy. Coverage changes by brand.

Energy Star attic targets for an uninsulated attic are a good starting point.

| Climate zone | Attic, uninsulated | Attic, 3 to 4 in existing | Floor |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | R-30 to R-49 | R-25 to R-30 | R-13 |
| 2 | R-30 to R-60 | R-25 to R-38 | R-13 to R-19 |
| 3 | R-30 to R-60 | R-25 to R-38 | R-19 to R-25 |
| 4 | R-38 to R-60 | R-38 | R-25 to R-30 |
| 5 to 8 | R-49 to R-60 | R-38 to R-49 | R-25 to R-30 |

For blown-in fiberglass, one published chart lists 22.2 bags per 1,000 sq ft to reach R-49 at about 16 3/4 in deep, and 28 bags per 1,000 sq ft for R-60. A cellulose and fiberglass chart from Knauf lists 26.4 bags per 1,000 sq ft for R-49 and 20 bags per 1,000 sq ft for R-38. Pick one product, use its chart, and stay with it for the whole job.

For batts, label coverage is just as direct. One Knauf R-19 batt bag sold at Home Depot covers 110.42 sq ft. An R-19 batt fits a 2 x 6 wall or a floor. It does not reach an attic target on its own, so attic batts are normally laid in two crossed layers.

## Worked example: a 1,000 sq ft attic to R-49

Say your attic floor is 25 x 40 ft (7.6 x 12.2 m), the attic has no insulation, and you are in Zone 5. Your target is R-49. You plan to rent a blower and use the Knauf blown-in chart.

Step 1: Area = 25 x 40 = 1,000 sq ft.

Step 2: Chart rate for R-49 = 26.4 bags per 1,000 sq ft.

Step 3: Bags = 1,000 / 1,000 x 26.4 = 26.4 bags.

Step 4: Round up like a buyer. You cannot buy 0.4 of a bag, so buy 27 bags.

Check the math a second way. The same chart says one bag covers no more than 37.8 sq ft at R-49. Bags = 1,000 / 37.8 = 26.46 bags. That rounds up to 27 bags. Both methods agree.

Depth check: that chart calls for about 16 3/8 in of settled depth for R-49. Staple paper rulers to a few joists before you start. Blow to the ruler, not to a guess.

If you used batts instead, the math changes. Area 1,000 sq ft divided by 110.42 sq ft per R-19 bag = 9.06 bags per layer. Round up to 10 bags per layer. Two crossed layers give about R-38. A third partial layer or a thicker batt is needed to pass R-49, which is why most attic jobs use blown-in.

## How to measure what you already have

Push a ruler down to the ceiling drywall in five or six spots. Use the lowest common depth, not the fluffiest spot. Old loose fiberglass is worth roughly R-2.2 to R-2.7 per inch. Old cellulose is worth roughly R-2.9 to R-3.4 per inch.

Say you find 6 in of old cellulose. That is about 6 x 3.1 = R-19. If your target is R-49, you need about R-30 more. On the Knauf chart, R-30 takes 15.3 bags per 1,000 sq ft, rounded up to 16 bags.

Do not bury problems. Wet, moldy, or pest-damaged insulation should come out first. If you see vermiculite, the gray pebble-like fill in some older homes, stop and get it tested before you disturb it. It can contain asbestos.

## Batts or blown-in: which fits your space?

Batts suit open stud walls, floors over a crawl space, and small attic sections you can walk. Cut them to fit with a utility knife and a straight board. Gaps around wires and pipes are the weak point. Cut around obstructions, do not stuff a batt into a tight bay. Compression lowers the R-value.

Blown-in suits most attics. It fills around joists, wires, and truss webs with fewer gaps. It needs a blower, a helper to feed bags, and depth markers. Many stores lend the blower free with a minimum bag purchase. Ask about the threshold before you buy.

For walls in a finished room, neither option is simple. Blown-in through drilled holes is a pro job with a dense-pack machine. If the room is already open, pair this job with our [drywall calculator](/blog/drywall-calculator/) so wall material is planned at the same time.

## Mistakes that waste money

The first mistake is buying to a depth, not a bag count. A thin spread can look deep and still miss the R-value. Count the empty bags as you go.

The second mistake is skipping air sealing. Seal top plates, wire holes, plumbing stacks, and the attic hatch before you insulate. Insulation slows heat flow. It does not stop air leaks.

The third mistake is blocking soffit vents. Fit baffles at the eaves so air can move to the ridge vents. Insulation pushed tight at the eave can cause moisture trouble and ice dams.

The fourth mistake is stepping between ceiling joists and cracking the drywall below. Lay planks across the joists to move around.

## When to hire a pro

Hire a pro if the attic has vermiculite, knob-and-tube wiring, a very low pitch, or signs of roof leaks. Hire one too for dense-pack wall work or spray foam at the rim joist. Get the quote in bags, settled depth, and target R-value, not just a total price. Check the bag count with the formula above before you sign.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many bags of blown-in insulation do I need for 1,000 sq ft?
At R-49, plan on about 27 bags using the Knauf chart rate of 26.4 bags per 1,000 sq ft, rounded up. A fiberglass product chart lists 22.2 bags per 1,000 sq ft for R-49. Always use the chart for the brand in your cart.

### What R-value do I need in my attic?
Energy Star lists R-30 to R-49 for Zone 1 and R-49 to R-60 for Zones 5 to 8 in an uninsulated attic. Most homes in the middle of the country land at R-49. Check your zone and your local code before you buy.

### Can I add new insulation over old insulation?
Yes, if the old layer is dry, clean, and free of mold and pests. R-values add together, so a sound R-19 layer plus R-30 of new material gives about R-49. Do not add a second faced layer with the facing trapped in the middle.

### How deep is R-49 blown-in insulation?
About 16 3/8 in settled depth on the Knauf fiberglass chart, and about 16 3/4 in for the Owens Corning ProPink product noted above. Depth changes by material, so read the chart on your bag and blow to depth markers.

### Do batts or blown-in cost less?
Batts often cost less per bag for small, open areas and need no machine. Blown-in usually wins in a full attic because it fills gaps and the blower is often free with a bag purchase. Compare cost per sq ft at the same R-value, not cost per bag.
